title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums`. For every index `i`, look only at the elements that sit at indices greater than `i` and count how many of them are strictly less than `nums[i]` (equal values do not count).

Return an array `counts` with the same length as `nums`, where `counts[i]` holds that count for index `i`. The last element always gets `0`.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct method compares every element with everything after it, which is O(n²) and too slow for 10^5 values. Turn it around: walk from the right end to the left, so that when you reach index `i`, exactly the elements after it have been seen. The question becomes "how many seen values are below `nums[i]`?", a prefix count over values. A binary indexed (Fenwick) tree keyed by value answers that prefix count and records a new value, each in O(log n).

## Approach

1. Collect the distinct values in `sorted` and give each a 1-based `rank` (coordinate compression), so the tree has one slot per distinct value.
2. Create `tree` with `sorted.length + 1` zeros and an answer array `counts`.
3. Visit `i` from the last index down to 0.
4. Query: start `index` at `rank(nums[i]) - 1` and add up `tree[index]` while stripping the lowest set bit; the total `smaller` counts seen values with a strictly lower rank.
5. Store `smaller` in `counts[i]`.
6. Update: start `index` at `rank(nums[i])` and add 1 to `tree[index]` while adding the lowest set bit, so later queries include this value.
7. Return `counts`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [5, 2, 6, 1]` gives `sorted = [1, 2, 5, 6]` with ranks 1, 2, 3, 4.

- `i = 3` (value 1, rank 1): the query starts at 0, so `smaller = 0`. Record rank 1.
- `i = 2` (value 6, rank 4): the prefix up to rank 3 holds only the 1, so `smaller = 1`. Record rank 4.
- `i = 1` (value 2, rank 2): the prefix up to rank 1 holds the 1, so `smaller = 1`. Record rank 2.
- `i = 0` (value 5, rank 3): the prefix up to rank 2 holds 1 and 2, so `smaller = 2`.

The answer is `[2, 1, 1, 0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): sorting the distinct values, plus one query and one update of O(log n) per element.
- Space: O(n) for `sorted`, `rank`, `tree` and `counts`.

## Pitfalls

- Query the prefix that ends one rank below `nums[i]`; querying up to its own rank would also count equal values.
- Query before you update, or the element would count itself when duplicates are present.
- A Fenwick tree is 1-based: index 0 must never be updated, or `index & -index` is 0 and the loop never ends.
- Walking left to right counts smaller elements before each index, which is a different problem.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sorted` | the distinct values in increasing order |
| `rank` | map from a value to its 1-based position in `sorted` |
| `tree` | the Fenwick tree: partial counts of values already seen |
| `counts` | the answer array |
| `i` | the index being answered, moving right to left |
| `index` | the Fenwick position being read or updated |
| `smaller` | how many seen values have a lower rank than `nums[i]` |

narration.5: Give each distinct value a 1-based rank; the Fenwick tree cannot use slot 0.
narration.7: One tree slot per distinct value, plus the unused slot 0.
narration.10: Walk from right to left so the tree holds exactly the values after i.
narration.11: Start the query one rank below nums[i] so equal values are not counted.
narration.13: Keep reading while the position is still inside the tree.
narration.14: Add the partial count stored at this position.
narration.15: Strip the lowest set bit to jump to the next block of smaller ranks.
narration.17: Every seen value below nums[i] has been counted; that is the answer for i.
narration.18: Now record nums[i] itself, starting at its own rank.
narration.20: Each block that covers this rank gains one value.
narration.21: Add the lowest set bit to climb to the next block that covers this rank.
narration.24: Every index has its count of smaller values to its right.
